progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c10 (esters and esterification as an equilibrium); chem-m7-c13 (synthesis routes; each step loses product); chem-m5-c04b (catalysts); chem-m5-c07 (the industrial yield, rate and cost compromise); Module 5 equilibrium shifts; skills-s08 (PEEL and the judgement with a condition); Year 11 percentage yield and collision theory. Not assumed: the aspirin reaction, ethanoic anhydride, recrystallisation, the iron(III) chloride purity check.
progression.startsWith: In 1897, a chemist at Bayer in Germany made a pure sample of acetylsalicylic acid, and in 1899 it went on sale as Aspirin. More than a century later, a school lab can make a few grams in an afternoon, and factories make it by the tonne. So how do chemists decide on a recipe, and how do you judge whether it's a good one?
progression.stopsAfter: explaining each design factor for aspirin and how the factors trade off; transferring them to biodiesel and fuel ethanol; planning an evaluation with a judgement and its condition. No atom economy or E-factor calculations, no drug trials, no mechanisms.

teaching.task: Aspirin has been made for well over a century, by the gram at school and by the tonne in factories. How do chemists decide on a recipe, and how do you judge whether it's a good one?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why the anhydride: it makes no water, so nothing drives the reaction back, and it goes almost to completion (4). Why a catalyst and a warm bath: more collisions with enough energy, through a lower-energy pathway; the catalyst doesn't change where it ends (5, c04b recall). Why not hotter: side products, fumes, energy cost (5). Why yields fall short: product stays dissolved, sticks to glassware, stays on the paper (6). Why recrystallisation purifies: aspirin crystallises as the solution cools while most impurities stay dissolved (7). Why iron(III) chloride detects salicylic acid: salicylic acid has a free ring OH and aspirin's is an ester (7). Why the by-product needn't be waste: it can be turned back into anhydride (8). Why cost matters so much: a very low price per tablet (9). Why excess methanol: adding a reactant shifts an equilibrium to the products (feedback 1). Why a condition in the verdict: the judgement depends on recovery and purification, or on cheap energy for distillation (10, feedback 2).
teaching.conversationalApproach: In 1897, a chemist at Bayer in Germany made a pure sample of acetylsalicylic acid, and in 1899 it went on sale as Aspirin. Here's the reaction. Before anything else, you need the reagents, in bulk. Why not use plain ethanoic acid, the acid in vinegar? It can make the same ester, but that reaction is an equilibrium. Next, speed. Now, how much do you get? Yield compares the aspirin you collect with the most the equation says you could make. A medicine has to be pure, and leftover salicylic acid can irritate the stomach. Then safety and waste. Finally, step back. So how do you judge it? As in the extended responses video, decide the verdict first, then give each factor a paragraph with its evidence. One line to keep: yield tells you how much product you collected, not how good the route is. Your turn. The reaction is an equilibrium, so adding extra methanol, a reactant, shifts it towards the products and converts more of the oil. Last one, and it's a long response. One strong plan starts with the verdict. So for any synthesis, ask where the reagents come from, which conditions balance speed, yield and cost, how pure the product must be, how safe it is and what it wastes, and who it serves at what cost.

Crossed mistake: "excess methanol mainly makes it faster". Crossed mistake: a list of advantages and disadvantages with no verdict (s08's crossed habit, now applied). - environmental, social and economic issues"

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. Question card (tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), worded as printed: "A company in Queensland, close to sugar-cane farms and mills, plans to produce ethanol for fuel. It is considering two routes. Route 1, hydration of ethene: ethene made from crude oil reacts with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 °C and 60 to 70 atm; the reaction is reversible; the process runs continuously; ethanol is separated from water and unreacted gas is recycled. Route 2, fermentation: yeast ferments sugar from cane molasses at about 30 to 35 °C without oxygen; each batch takes days and stops at about 15% ethanol, so the ethanol must be distilled, which uses energy; sugar mills can burn cane waste to supply this energy; the carbon dioxide released is taken up again by the next crop of cane as it grows. Evaluate the two routes for this company. (7 marks)" Below it, the task line: "Plan your answer: a verdict, then one line per paragraph." m7-sugarcane-stalks-v1.png and m7-crude-oil-barrel-v1.png small at the card's right. Revision 2 (learning L1): the card writes on in full first, then a silent reading hold of about 8 s (no narration, no ring; small grey tag "read the question") before the narration starts. The full question stays on screen. After "Pause here to answer." the countdown ring runs 10 seconds with "Pause here to answer." and a grey tag "longer task: pause the video and take about a minute". Nothing answer-bearing.
